claim: Hair cells transduce mechanical stimuli into electrical responses and initiate the perception of sounds and accelerations.
source: Hair cells occur universally in the auditory and vestibular systems of vertebrates, where they transduce mechanical stimuli into electrical responses and thus initiate the perception of sounds and accelerations (Hudspeth, 2008, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hudspeth 2008 and 2014

claim: The apical surface of a hair cell bears a hair bundle comprising actin-filled stereocilia whose gradation in height forms a bevel.
source: The apical surface of a hair cell bears a hair bundle comprising actin-filled stereocilia whose gradation in height forms a bevel (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and established knowledge of hair cell structure

claim: The tip of each stereocilium is connected to the side of the tallest adjacent stereocilium through a protein filament called the tip link.
source: The tip of each stereocilium is connected to the side of the tallest adjacent stereocilium through a protein filament, the tip link (Pickles et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickles et al., 1984

claim: The upper two-thirds of the tip link comprises a parallel dimer of cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules.
source: The upper two-thirds of this link comprises a parallel dimer of cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules whereas the lower third encompasses a parallel dimer of protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kazmierczak et al., 2007

claim: The lower third of the tip link encompasses a parallel dimer of protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules.
source: The upper two-thirds of this link comprises a parallel dimer of cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules whereas the lower third encompasses a parallel dimer of protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kazmierczak et al., 2007

claim: Deflection of a hair bundle toward its tall edge opens mechanoelectrical-transduction channels that allow an influx of cations, predominantly K+ but also Ca2+, and thus depolarizes the hair cell.
source: Deflection of a hair bundle toward its tall edge opens mechanoelectrical-transduction channels that allow an influx of cations, predominantly K+ but also Ca2+, and thus depolarizes the hair cell.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of hair cell physiology

claim: Deflection increases the tension in an elastic structure called the gating spring that communicates force to the transduction channels.
source: Electrophysiological and mechanical evidence suggests that deflection increases the tension in an elastic structure, the gating spring, that communicates force to the transduction channels (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a

claim: The stereociliary tips are the site of transduction.
source: Several lines of circumstantial evidence support the hypothesis that the tip link constitutes at least a portion of the gating spring: the stereociliary tips are the site of transduction (Hudspeth, 1982; Beurg et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hudspeth, 1982 and Beurg et al., 2009

claim: The orientation of the tip links corresponds to the hair bundle's axis of maximal sensitivity.
source: the orientation of the tip links corresponds to the hair bundle's axis of maximal sensitivity (Shotwell et al., 1981)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shotwell et al., 1981

claim: The responsiveness vanishes when the tip links are disrupted.
source: and the responsiveness vanishes when the tip links are disrupted (Assad et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Assad et al., 1991

claim: The critical role of tip-link tension in gating mechanoelectrical-transduction channels has never been tested directly.
source: Nevertheless, the critical role of tip-link tension in gating mechanoelectrical-transduction channels has never been tested directly.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this study

claim: Tip links occur in the narrow spaces between the tips of contiguous stereocilia and are not readily accessible to experimental manipulation.
source: Because they occur in the narrow spaces between the tips of contiguous stereocilia, tip links are not readily accessible to experimental manipulation.
evidence: Based on knowledge of hair bundle structure and inference about experimental accessibility

claim: The stimulation of transduction channels has heretofore been limited to the deflection of entire hair bundles.
source: As a consequence, the stimulation of transduction channels has heretofore been limited to the deflection of entire hair bundles.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this study

claim: A polyclonal antiserum was raised against a specific epitope near the carboxyl terminal of the bullfrog's CDH23.
source: To apply tension at a defined position on each of a large number of tip links, we raised a polyclonal antiserum against a specific epitope near the carboxyl terminal of the bullfrog's CDH23, and thus at the links' upper ends.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in this study

claim: A mechanical tether for the tip link was created by interposing a 3 kb, double-stranded DNA molecule between the attached antibody and a 1 μm-diameter superparamagnetic bead.
source: We therefore created a mechanical tether for the tip link by interposing a 3 kb, double-stranded DNA molecule between the attached antibody and a 1 μm-diameter superparamagnetic bead (Figure 1B).
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in this study, with reference to Figure 1B

claim: The DNA molecule was obtained by PCR of a plasmid with primers that incorporated biotin and fluorescein moieties at the molecule's opposite ends.
source: The DNA molecule was obtained by PCR of a plasmid with primers that incorporated biotin and fluorescein moieties at the molecule's opposite ends.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in this study

claim: The biotinylated terminus bound through a streptavidin molecule to a biotinylated anti-rabbit IgG, which in turn bound the rabbit anti-CDH23.
source: The biotinylated terminus bound through a streptavidin molecule to a biotinylated anti-rabbit IgG, which in turn bound the rabbit anti-CDH23.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in this study

claim: The fluorescein-modified end of the DNA adhered to a superparamagnetic bead coated with anti-fluorescein.
source: The fluorescein-modified end of the DNA adhered to a superparamagnetic bead coated with anti-fluorescein.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in this study

claim: The tether provided sufficient separation between the tip link and the relatively large bead to overcome the problem of steric inaccessibility.
source: The tether provided sufficient separation between the tip link and the relatively large bead to overcome the problem of steric inaccessibility.
evidence: Inference about the function of the DNA tether based on its design

claim: The anti-CDH23 antibodies labeled the stereociliary tips in living hair cells of the bullfrog's sacculus.
source: First, the anti-CDH23 antibodies labeled the stereociliary tips in living hair cells of the bullfrog's sacculus (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: The antibodies' binding to cadherin isoforms was confirmed for both saccular and brain tissue by Western blot analysis.
source: The antibodies' binding to cadherin isoforms was also confirmed for both saccular and brain tissue by Western blot analysis.
evidence: Experimental observation from Western blot analysis

claim: Following synthesis of the complete tether, superparamagnetic beads localized to the regions of the tip links.
source: Following synthesis of the complete tether, superparamagnetic beads localized to the regions of the tip links but were absent if the primary antibody, secondary antibody, or streptavidin was omitted during the process of tether synthesis (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: Superparamagnetic beads were absent if the primary antibody, secondary antibody, or streptavidin was omitted during the process of tether synthesis.
source: Following synthesis of the complete tether, superparamagnetic beads localized to the regions of the tip links but were absent if the primary antibody, secondary antibody, or streptavidin was omitted during the process of tether synthesis (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Experimental observation from control experiments shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: Treatment of the preparation with DNAse liberated the superparamagnetic beads.
source: Finally, as expected for DNA tethers, treatment of the preparation with DNAse liberated the superparamagnetic beads.
evidence: Experimental observation confirming DNA tether function

claim: Pulling the tip links upward with magnetic force elicited ionic currents into the hair cells and produced a transepithelial electrical response termed the microphonic potential.
source: If an increase in tip-link tension opens mechanoelectrical-transduction channels, pulling the links upward should elicit ionic currents into the hair cells and thus produce a transepithelial electrical response termed the microphonic potential (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983b).
evidence: Hypothesis tested in the experiment, with citation to Corey and Hudspeth, 1983b

claim: Upon the application of current through the electromagnet in either direction, electrical responses were observed whose polarity was consistent with inward cationic currents through the apical surfaces of the hair cells.
source: Upon the application of current through the electromagnet in either direction, we observed electrical responses whose polarity was consistent with inward cationic currents through the apical surfaces of the hair cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2B

claim: In the presence of 1 mM gentamicin, only small, magnetically induced artifacts were detected during stimulation of either polarity.
source: To confirm that these signals originated primarily from transduction channels, we conducted control experiments in the presence of 1 mM gentamicin, a blocker of transduction channels (Kroese et al., 1989). We then detected only small, magnetically induced artifacts during stimulation of either polarity.
evidence: Experimental observation from control experiments with gentamicin, with citation to Kroese et al., 1989

claim: No response was observed when the primary antiserum was omitted from the preparative procedure.
source: Moreover, no response was observed when the primary antiserum was omitted from the preparative procedure.
evidence: Experimental observation from control experiments

claim: The pulling force on a superparamagnetic bead does not depend on the direction of the current through the electromagnet.
source: Because the pulling force on a superparamagnetic bead does not depend on the direction of the current through the electromagnet, the physiological responses to stimuli of opposite polarities should have been identical.
evidence: Based on knowledge of superparamagnetic bead behavior in magnetic fields

claim: The artifacts should have reversed signs in accordance with Faraday's law.
source: The artifacts, however, should have reversed signs in accordance with Faraday's law.
evidence: Based on knowledge of electromagnetic induction

claim: By averaging the responses to stimuli of opposite polarities, artifacts were removed and only the responses owing to mechanoelectrical transduction were preserved.
source: To separate the transduction responses from artifacts, we therefore applied to the magnet successive voltage pulses of a constant magnitude but opposite polarities. By averaging the responses to these two stimuli we removed the artifacts and preserved only the responses owing to mechanoelectrical transduction (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental method and observation shown in Figure 2B

claim: The peak response in nine experiments was 38.7 ± 9.8 μV (mean ± standard deviation).
source: The peak response in nine experiments was 38.7 ± 9.8 μV (mean ± standard deviation), roughly one-tenth the maximal value expected if every tip link were stimulated.
evidence: Experimental measurement from nine experiments

claim: The peak response was roughly one-tenth the maximal value expected if every tip link were stimulated.
source: The peak response in nine experiments was 38.7 ± 9.8 μV (mean ± standard deviation), roughly one-tenth the maximal value expected if every tip link were stimulated.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data to theoretical expectation

claim: Gentamicin treatment revealed that the residual artifacts were equal and opposite and summed to zero.
source: As expected, gentamicin treatment revealed that the residual artifacts were equal and opposite and summed to zero.
evidence: Experimental observation from control experiments with gentamicin

claim: The signals elicited by conventional hair-bundle deflection adapt rapidly to a plateau.
source: Although the signals elicited by conventional hair-bundle deflection adapt rapidly to a plateau (Eatock et al., 1987; Shepherd and Corey, 1994), the responses elicited by protracted magnetic stimulation declined gradually over several seconds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eatock et al., 1987 and Shepherd and Corey, 1994

claim: The responses elicited by protracted magnetic stimulation declined gradually over several seconds.
source: Although the signals elicited by conventional hair-bundle deflection adapt rapidly to a plateau (Eatock et al., 1987; Shepherd and Corey, 1994), the responses elicited by protracted magnetic stimulation declined gradually over several seconds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2C

claim: Conventional stimulation of a hair bundle is thought to tense each tip link and open the associated channels.
source: Conventional stimulation of a hair bundle is thought to tense each tip link and open the associated channels.
evidence: Statement of established hypothesis in the field

claim: Aided by the effect of Ca2+ on the myosin molecules that secure the upper ends of the tip links, tension declines, resulting in adaptation of the electrical response.
source: Aided by the effect of Ca2+ on the myosin molecules that secure the upper ends of the tip links, this tension then declines, resulting in adaptation of the electrical response (Howard and Hudspeth, 1987; Assad et al., 1989; Hacohen et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Howard and Hudspeth, 1987; Assad et al., 1989; Hacohen et al., 1989

claim: Magnetic stimulation pulls the top ends of the tip links upward and not only opens transduction channels but evidently restrains the insertional plaques from descending.
source: Magnetic stimulation, in contrast, should pull the top ends of the tip links upward. This force not only opened transduction channels but evidently restrained the insertional plaques from descending as well.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations about the mechanism of magnetic stimulation

claim: Recovery from the vertical offset of the plaques might explain why the electrical response relaxed far more slowly than during conventional adaptation.
source: Recovery from the vertical offset of the plaques might explain why the electrical response relaxed far more slowly than during conventional adaptation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed phenomenon

claim: The magnitude of the response was sensitive to the strength of magnetic stimulation.
source: Because the magnitude of the response was sensitive to the strength of magnetic stimulation, the long plateau observed during protracted magnetic stimulation did not stem from saturation of the response.
evidence: Experimental observation

claim: The long plateau observed during protracted magnetic stimulation did not stem from saturation of the response.
source: Because the magnitude of the response was sensitive to the strength of magnetic stimulation, the long plateau observed during protracted magnetic stimulation did not stem from saturation of the response.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation

claim: With the beads localized to one region with similar hair-bundle orientations, magnetic force pulls those bundles upward and toward their short edges.
source: With the beads localized to one region with similar hair-bundle orientations, magnetic force pulls those bundles upward and toward their short edges.
evidence: Description of experimental condition in tilted preparation

claim: An electrical response persisted after removal of most beads in the tilted preparation.
source: Even under these conditions we observed a transduction current of the usual polarity but of diminished magnitude owing to the removal of most tethered beads (Figure 2F).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2F

claim: The response vanished when the remaining beads had been scraped away.
source: As expected, the response vanished when the remaining beads had been scraped away.
evidence: Experimental observation from control experiment

claim: Treatment with 1 mM EGTA dissociates tip links.
source: To eliminate this possibility, we dissociated tip links by treatment with 1 mM EGTA.
evidence: Based on knowledge of EGTA's effect on tip links

claim: After treatment with 1 mM EGTA, the summed response fell to zero.
source: Under these conditions the summed response fell to zero (Figure 2G), indicating that the responses stemmed from traction on tip links.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2G

claim: The responses stemmed from traction on tip links.
source: Under these conditions the summed response fell to zero (Figure 2G), indicating that the responses stemmed from traction on tip links.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation with EGTA treatment

claim: Upward force on tip links generates transduction currents independent of hair-bundle deflection.
source: By overcoming this limitation, our experiments have demonstrated that upward force on tip links generates transduction currents independent of hair-bundle deflection.
evidence: Main conclusion from experimental observations

claim: These responses vanish in the presence of a channel blocker.
source: As expected, these responses vanish in the presence of a channel blocker.
evidence: Experimental observation from gentamicin control experiments

claim: The observed responses accord well with the values expected on the basis of the calibrated magnetic force on tethered beads and the gating-spring theory for transduction by hair cells.
source: The observed responses accord well with the values expected on the basis of the calibrated magnetic force on tethered beads and the gating-spring theory for transduction by hair cells.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data to theoretical predictions

claim: The present observations provide direct support for the hypothesis that tension in gating springs within the hair bundle opens transduction channels.
source: More than three decades after the postulation that tension in gating springs within the hair bundle opens transduction channels (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a) and the subsequent suggestion that tip links constitute those elements (Pickles et al., 1984), the present observations provide direct support for both hypotheses.
evidence: Main conclusion from experimental observations, with citations to Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a and Pickles et al., 1984

claim: The present observations provide direct support for the hypothesis that tip links constitute the gating springs.
source: More than three decades after the postulation that tension in gating springs within the hair bundle opens transduction channels (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a) and the subsequent suggestion that tip links constitute those elements (Pickles et al., 1984), the present observations provide direct support for both hypotheses.
evidence: Main conclusion from experimental observations, with citations to Corey and Hudspeth, 1983a and Pickles et al., 1984

claim: The technical approach introduced here affords a means of investigating mechanoelectrical transduction at the scale of individual tip links and channels.
source: The technical approach introduced here additionally affords a means of investigating mechanoelectrical transduction at the scale of individual tip links and channels.
evidence: Inference about future applications of the method

claim: The epitope selected for the antiserum corresponds to the Ca2+-binding linker between extracellular cadherin domains EC25 and EC26 of the murine CDH23 protein.
source: Wishing to develop an antiserum against an epitope of the bullfrog's CDH23 near the upper insertion of the tip link, we selected the region corresponding to the Ca2+-binding linker between extracellular cadherin domains EC25 and EC26 of the murine protein (UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot: Q99PF4.2).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to protein database

claim: This region was selected on the basis of its probable accessibility and antigenicity and because it occurs near the uppermost of CDH23's 27 extracellular cadherin domains.
source: This region was selected on the basis of its probable accessibility and antigenicity and because it occurs near the uppermost of CDH23's 27 extracellular cadherin domains.

source: Using primers based on the DNA sequence for the zebrafish's cdh23 (NM_214809), we obtained a product by RT-PCR of the RNA isolated from a single bullfrog's sacculus (Superscript III One-Step RT-PCR System, Invitrogen).
